title: Vera: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale
hook: Testing agent safety by hand doesn't scale — Vera automates the whole pipeline and finds a 93.9% average attack success rate across four production agent frameworks.
key_points: Vera is a three-stage automated pipeline: discover emerging risks from literature, combine them into executable 'safety cases,' then run agents against those cases in sandboxes.
Verification is evidence-grounded — judged from environment state and tool-call logs, not the agent's own self-report of what it did.
Evaluated on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code): average attack success rate hit 93.9% under multi-channel attacks.
Released Vera-Bench: 1,600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings.
Pitch: hard-coded safety rules can't keep up with fast-evolving agents; testing infrastructure needs to be modular and automated too.
content_html: Testing whether an AI agent is safe used to mean hand-writing rules for known bad behaviors — expensive, and always a step behind as agents evolve. Vera automates the entire safety-testing loop instead.
extra_html:
Vera runs a self-reinforcing three-stage pipeline: it first mines the literature to build taxonomies of emerging risks, attack methods, and tool environments; then combinatorially composes those taxonomy dimensions into concrete "safety cases," each with a goal, a programmatic starting state, and a verification predicate; then executes those cases against real agents in isolated sandboxes, with a control agent steering the multi-turn interaction and evidence-grounded verifiers judging outcomes from environment state and tool-call logs rather than trusting the agent's own account of what happened.

Run against four production agent frameworks — OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, and Claude Code — Vera surfaced substantial safety weaknesses, with an average attack success rate of 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. The authors also release Vera-Bench, 1,600 executable safety cases across 124 risk categories and three execution settings, arguing that testing infrastructure for agents needs to be as modular and automated as the agents themselves. Yunhao Feng et al., arXiv 2026.

related.title: OpenSkillRisk: Benchmarking Agent Safety with Risky Third-Party Skills
related.hook: Give an AI agent a third-party 'skill' and even the safest setups still run unsafe actions about 17% of the time — a benchmark of 263 risky skills shows exactly how they slip through.

related.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
related.hook: Finding the prompts that make a model misbehave is slow if humans do it by hand. So use another language model to generate those attacks automatically — at scale.

related.title: When Claws Remember but Do Not Tell: Stealthy Memory Injection
related.hook: One poisoned email is enough: this attack tricks a persistent personal agent into silently writing false memories, hiding the evidence from the user, and acting on the lie later.

related.title: Untrusted Content Masking: A Trust Boundary for Web Agents
related.hook: Provable prompt-injection defenses rely on never letting an agent read untrusted content directly. Web agents break that just by looking at the page — this restores it via the page's own structure.

related.title: Agentic Abstention: Do Agents Know When to Stop?
related.hook: Across 28,000+ tasks, agents often can't tell when to quit — some never give up when they should, others bail out only after dozens of wasted tool calls.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Vera judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence instead of the agent's own report?
flashcards.back_html: An agent's self-report of what it did can't be trusted as a safety signal — a compromised or manipulated agent might misreport. Grounding verification in observable artifacts (files changed, calls made) gives a deterministic, tamper-resistant check.

flashcards.prompt: What did Vera find when testing OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, and Claude Code?

choices.text: Average attack success rate of 93.9% under multi-channel attacks
All four frameworks blocked every tested attack
Only one of the four frameworks showed any vulnerability

flashcards.explanation_html: Vera's evaluation across all four production agent frameworks revealed substantial, widespread safety weaknesses, not an isolated issue.

flashcards.back_html: A released benchmark of 1,600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings, generated by Vera's combinatorial safety-case pipeline.
